Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
 i need a prompt for someone to write the spoken text for a small audio guide at Bellwether City Museum. the exhibition is called “Small Weather: Objects for Listening,” and it runs from 12 April to 30 August 2027. this is for visitors walking through the show on their own, not a live tour. The guide should have six stops in the room order below and take about seven or eight minutes to hear, around 650 to 750 words altogether. make it clear enough for visitors aged 12 and up who are not specialists, without sounding like a school worksheet. use English. i want the narration to feel attentive and human, not grand or salesy, with pauses only where they help someone look or listen.

The six stops are already decided, so keep this order: the brass rain gauge, the slate weather board, the glass storm lantern, Mara Ell’s textile, the harbor sound recording, and the listening bench. Please give each stop a short spoken heading and a useful transition to the next one; there is no need for a separate introduction that uses up a whole stop. At the first stop, mention that the exhibition is about the ways people have noticed, recorded, and remembered weather, rather than a history of forecasting equipment. The objects come from different years and uses, so don’t imply they were all made for one collection or one project. It would be good if the visitor can understand how each object relates to listening or noticing, but don’t force every stop to make the same point in the same words.

For the rain gauge, the object is a brass gauge made by Leena Vale in 1912. It was used on the roof of North Quay School, and its scale is marked only up to 40 millimeters. The Vale family donated it to the museum in 1986. Please don’t claim that it records a particular storm or that its upper mark tells us exactly how much rain fell on any one day; the information here is just the maker, date, use, scale, and donation. It might be worth letting listeners picture the gauge on a school roof, but not inventing what anyone saw from there. The second stop is a slate weather board used by a school caretaker whose name is not known. It has chalk tallies for each month from October 1918 through February 1919. The records are monthly tallies, not daily readings, and we don’t know who made each mark. Keep those limits clear, perhaps by saying what the board can show and what it cannot. don’t turn the unknown caretaker into a named person or add a story about the school during those months.

The third object is a glass storm lantern made by H. Orr & Sons in 1936. A ferry keeper used it on the breakwater. That is the extent of the information about its use: don’t say it was carried during a particular storm, rescue, or crossing. For the textile stop, Mara Ell made “Tide Map” in 1974 from cotton sailcloth. It came from three walks she took after the 1972 flood. The colors are not a measured scale for water depth, so don’t explain them as if blue or dark thread marks a specific depth. You can invite the listener to look at how the stitched paths sit across the sailcloth, but please don’t make up the places the walks went or claim they are a literal map of the flood. These two objects should remain distinct: one is a lantern with a stated working use, the other is an artwork made from the artist’s walks.

The fifth stop is a harbor sound recording made in 1989 by museum staff member Daniel Rusk. It is 42 seconds long and contains a ferry horn, rope moving against a metal post, and gulls. The recording was made from the museum’s east pier, but no exact time of day is documented. Please do not identify a specific ferry, bird, or weather condition from the sound. A visitor at a 2024 family day said, “I thought the gauge would tell us how hard the rain fell.” That is an ordinary visitor comment from the museum’s notes; if there is room, use it once as a brief quoted moment, and don’t present it as a scientific conclusion. The last stop is the listening bench, a plain oak bench installed in the gallery for this exhibition. It has no recording or interactive controls. It is there so visitors can sit and listen to the harbor recording again if they want. This is an allowed action: you may invite visitors to sit there or replay the recording.

Please shape the guide as spoken narration, not a wall label or a catalogue entry. Keep each stop focused on the supplied facts, and use sensory language only where the object or recording supports it. Avoid inventing dialogue, motives, measurements, biographies, or museum history. Do not make claims about what the objects prove, and don’t treat unknown details as settled. Don’t add a new object, a seventh stop, or a route outside these galleries. do not contact vendors. This means the writer should work from this brief rather than asking a supplier for more material; it does not mean to remove the existing objects or the museum-staff recording from the guide. We need the narration itself, not a production plan or equipment recommendations. End with a simple invitation to continue through the exhibition after the bench, without summing up the whole show or declaring what visitors should have learned.", "output": "Write spoken narration for a six-stop audio guide to Bellwether City Museum’s exhibition “Small Weather: Objects for Listening,” open from 12 April to 30 August 2027. The guide is for visitors aged 12 and up exploring on their own. Use clear English and an attentive, human tone that is neither grand nor salesy. Aim for about seven or eight minutes, or 650–750 words in total. Include brief spoken headings and useful transitions, following the room order below. Do not use a separate introduction that takes up a stop.

Introduce the exhibition as being about how people have noticed, recorded, and remembered weather, rather than as a history of forecasting equipment. The objects come from different years and uses; do not suggest that they were made for one collection or project. Help visitors see how each object relates to noticing or listening without repeating the same point at every stop. Write narration, not wall labels, catalogue entries, a production plan, or equipment recommendations. Use sensory language only where supported by the facts. Do not invent dialogue, motives, measurements, biographies, museum history, or settled explanations for unknown details. Do not add objects, stops, or a route outside these galleries.

1. **Brass rain gauge:** The gauge was made by Leena Vale in 1912, used on the roof of North Quay School, and donated to the museum by the Vale family in 1986. Its scale is marked only up to 40 millimeters. You may invite listeners to picture it on the school roof, but do not invent what anyone saw there. Do not claim it records a particular storm or that its upper mark establishes how much rain fell on a specific day.

2. **Slate weather board:** A school caretaker whose name is not known used the board. Its chalk tallies cover each month from October 1918 through February 1919. These are monthly tallies, not daily readings, and the person who made each mark is unknown. Make clear what the board can show and what it cannot. Do not name the caretaker or invent a story about the school during those months.

3. **Glass storm lantern:** H. Orr & Sons made the lantern in 1936. A ferry keeper used it on the breakwater. Do not associate it with a particular storm, rescue, or crossing.

4. **Mara Ell’s textile:** Ell made “Tide Map” in 1974 from cotton sailcloth. It came from three walks she took after the 1972 flood. Its colors are not a measured scale for water depth. You may draw attention to the stitched paths across the sailcloth, but do not invent where the walks went or describe the textile as a literal map of the flood. Keep this artwork distinct from the lantern, which has a stated working use.

5. **Harbor sound recording:** Museum staff member Daniel Rusk made this 42-second recording in 1989 from the museum’s east pier. It contains a ferry horn, rope moving against a metal post, and gulls. No exact time of day is documented. Do not identify a particular ferry, bird, or weather condition from the sound. If room permits, include this visitor comment from a 2024 family day once: “I thought the gauge would tell us how hard the rain fell.” Present it as an ordinary visitor comment, not a scientific conclusion.

6. **Listening bench:** This plain oak bench was installed in the gallery for the exhibition. It has no recording or interactive controls. Visitors may sit and listen to the harbor recording again if they want. End with a simple invitation to continue through the exhibition after the bench; do not summarize the whole show or declare what visitors should have learned.

Do not contact vendors. Work from the information in this brief rather than asking a supplier for more material. This restriction does not remove any listed object or the museum-staff recording from the guide."}]
